books.section: Topic 6.7 Labor in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Harper’s Weekly engraving of the Haymarket Square bombing (May 15, 1886)

options.misconception: The engraving shows a blast, not who threw the bomb or planned it.
options.text: The Knights of Labor organized the bombing themselves.
The public came to link labor meetings with violence.

options.misconception: The engraving shows a meeting ending in a blast, not a victory.
options.text: The Knights won the eight-hour day at Haymarket.

options.misconception: The police are shown in the middle of the rally, not refusing to attend.
options.text: The police refused to attend any labor rallies.

rationales.A: The engraving shows a blast, not who threw the bomb or planned it.
rationales.B: The engraving shows a labor meeting ending in a bomb blast and police gunfire. Background from the books: after Haymarket, Americans linked unions with violence and the Knights lost members.
rationales.C: The engraving shows a meeting ending in a blast, not a victory for the eight-hour day.
rationales.D: The police are shown in the middle of the rally, not refusing to attend.
rationales.general:
Ask what a viewer of this picture would carry away.
1. The picture shows a labor meeting, a speaker, and a crowd.
2. It also shows a bomb blast, smoke, and men falling.
3. A viewer links the two: labor meetings and violence, side by side.
4. That link is what damaged the Knights in public eyes.
Remember: an image can show a link the public made, even when it proves nothing about who acted.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)
stem: The Haymarket bombing is often linked to the decline of the Knights of Labor. Which connection does the engraving best support?

stimulus.text: Harper’s Weekly engraving of the Haymarket Square bombing in Chicago, May 4, 1886. At the left, a speaker stands on a wagon with one arm raised, addressing the crowd. In the center, police officers move through thick smoke as the bomb explodes, and men fall and scatter in the street. A street sign on a building at the upper left reads “N. JEFFERSON ST.”
